profiles.name: Andrew Postaruk
profiles.description:
Andrew Postaruk was born 1881 in Kiev Governorate, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Worked as a laborer.

Previously emigrated to and worked in Austria and Germany. His wife and two children remained in Russia. 

In 1918 he joined the Union of Russian Workers in Seattle. He told authorities, “I don’t believe in any government,” but also “stated believe in change through the ballot as a I fear that bloodshed would ensue by bringing a revolution through force of arms.” Arrested January 1920 and deported to Russia February 1, 1921.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Bertha Zimmerman
profiles.description:
Bertha Zimmerman was born 1885 in Riga, Russia (present-day Latvia). Immigrated to the United States in 1907.

Born 1885, Riga, Russia (present-day Latvia). Latvian. Housewife; garment worker. Migrated to US 1907. Married fellow deportee David Zimmerman in Boston that same year. Literate in Russian, Lettish, German, and some English. Joined the National Lettish Organization of the Socialist Party of America. 1908 son Erick born. Circa 1908 moved to Chicago, where involved in the IWW. Circa 1918 moved to Baltimore. September 1919 charter member of the Lettish Federation of the Communist Party of America; member of the party’s Baltimore Central Committee and distributor of its publication The Communist. Arrested during the second Palmer Raids, January 2, 1920. Deported February 1, 1921.

INS file 54859/549; FBI file OG 391151

See also: Vernon L. Pedersen, The Communist Party in Maryland, 1919-57

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: David Davidovich Zimmerman
profiles.description:
David Davidovich Zimmerman was born 1875 in Riga, Russia (present-day Latvia). Immigrated to the United States in 1906.

Born 1875, Riga, Russia (present-day Latvia). Latvian. Carpenter. Circa 1904 joined the Latvian Social Democratic Workers’ Party. Migrated to US 1906. Joined the National Lettish Organization of the Socialist Party of America that year. Married fellow deportee Bertha Zimmerman in Boston 1907. 1908 son Erick born. Circa 1908 moved to Chicago, where involved in the IWW. Circa 1918 moved to Baltimore. September 1919 charter member of the Lettish Federation of the Communist Party of America; member of the party’s Baltimore Central Committee and distributor of its publication The Communist. Arrested during the second Palmer Raids, January 2, 1920. Deported February 1, 1921. 

Joined the Communist Party of the Soviet Union that same year. Lived in Leningrad. Arrested June 1938 for espionage during Stalin’s purges. Executed October 10, 1938.

INS file 54859/548; FBI file OG 46773

See also: Vernon L. Pedersen, The Communist Party in Maryland, 1919-57; https://ru.openlist.wiki/%D0%A6%D0%B8%D0%BC%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%BC%D0%B0%D0%BD_%D0%94%D0%B0%D0%B2%D0%B8%D0%B4_%D0%94%D0%B0%D0%B2%D0%B8%D0%B4%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87_(1875)

profiles.name: Frank L. Palmer
profiles.description: Frank L. Palmer was a labor journalist and editor prominent in 1920s Colorado. He edited the Colorado Labor Advocate, a Denver labor weekly, and was a correspondent for the Federated Press, the left-wing labor news service. During the 1927–1928 Colorado coal strike — the great walkout that culminated in the Columbine Mine Massacre, the killing of striking miners at Serene, Colorado in November 1927 — Palmer was a leading voice of the strikers, urging them to keep striking peacefully. He exposed corporate anti-union espionage in his 1928 book "Spies in Steel: An Exposé of Industrial War." A "fiery labor editor," he was, by a 1967 account, jailed more than once for his strike and organizing activity; that account also placed him in semi-retirement in Holland, Michigan, late in life. The specific charges, dates and sentences of his jailings are not documented in the readily available sources.

profiles.name: Ivan Anotsky
profiles.description:
Ivan Anotsky was born 1893 in Grodno Province, Russia (present-day Belarus). Worked as a porter. Immigrated to the United States in 1915.

Hoined Russian Branch No. 3 of the Socialist Party in Detroit around 1917, and transferred into the Communist Party of America at its founding in 1919. That same year he traveled to Pittsburgh to speak publicly against the anarchists of the Union of Russian Workers. Arrested in Detroit during the first Palmer Raids in January 1920, he was described by the city’s Review Committee of Citizens as educated, thrifty, hardworking, and of high intelligence. Deported to Russia on February 1, 1921. 

Upon arrival, he reportedly volunteered to help suppress the Kronstadt mutiny, afterward became a commissar, and ultimately fell into disfavor. One account claims he became an alcoholic and “degenerate,” and was sentenced to death for embezzlement, but escaped to Poland.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

Jacob K. Platek was born 1889 in Podolovka, Russia. Worked as a laborer, foundry worker. Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

His wife and child remained in Russia when he emigrated. He joined the Socialist Party and in 1919 became a member and financial secretary of Polish Branch No. 80 of the Communist Party in Grand Rapids, Michigan. Arrested January 2, 1920, he was deported to Poland August 4, 1920.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

Serving four years for organizing workers into the IWW, by his own account in the magazine.

profiles.name: Mike Matty
profiles.description:
Mike Matty was a coal miner from Brownsville, Pennsylvania, jailed at the Allegheny County Workhouse at Blawnox -- rendered in contemporary sources as "Blaw Knox" -- for National Miners Union activity during the 1928 soft-coal strike and his conflict with the John L. Lewis leadership of the United Mine Workers.

He was demonstrably in custody by October 1928 and was still imprisoned in January 1929. He was released on April 29, 1929, after what the contemporary defence publication called several months' imprisonment.

NO ADMISSION DATE IS RECORDED. October 1928 is the point at which custody is first attested, not the date he entered, so entering it would understate the term and present an attestation as an admission. His actual time served is therefore not calculated. The exact arrest, admission and sentencing dates, the formal charge and statute, the length of the sentence, his vital dates and any photograph are all unresolved.

profiles.name: Nuval Kerget
profiles.description:
Nuval Kerget was born 1875 in Minsk Governorate, Russia (present-day Belarus). Worked as a lumber worker. Immigrated to the United States in 1910.

First arrived in the United States through Honolulu in 1910 and later settled in Seattle in 1918. Worked as a lumber worker and became a member of the Union of Russian Workers as well as the Industrial Workers of the World in 1919. Arrested in January 1920 and deported to Russia on February 26, 1921.

profiles.name: Pavel Konavalchuk
profiles.description:
Pavel Konavalchuk was born 1894 in Russia. Immigrated to the United States in 1911.

A member of the Union of Russian Workers in Newark until the organization was broken up in November 1919. Arrested in Newark on January 3, 1920, he openly identified as an anarchist but stated his opposition to violence. Despite having a wife and American-born child in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, he was deported to Russia on February 26, 1921.

profiles.name: Robert Elstin
profiles.description:
Robert Elstin was born 1884 in Russia. Worked as a carpenter.

Entered Canada in 1913 as the “man servant” of Russian Consul General Basek, then migrated to the United States. Former member of the Russian branch of the Socialist Party; transferred in 1919 to Baltimore’s Lettish Branch of the Communist Party. Married, with wife Evelyn residing in the US. Arrested in Baltimore during the second Palmer Raids on January 2, 1920. Deported on February 1, 1921.

profiles.name: Thomas Harty
profiles.description:
Thomas Harty was one of the marine transport workers imprisoned at the Maine State Prison in Thomaston in the seamen's case of the early 1920s — the same prosecution that held Peter Dirks and Dan Fallon, already recorded in this database. His sentence was raised to seven to eleven years, and his letters appeared in the ILD's Labor Defender through 1927, which listed him on its roster of American class-war prisoners.

The June 1925 labor-press political-prisoner birthday notice lists him — as Tom Harty — at the Maine State Prison, Thomaston, with a June 17 birthday (no birth year is given).

profiles.description: Tony Stafford was an Italian-born union coal miner. Tony Stafford was imprisoned at the West Virginia penitentiary in Moundsville for his part in the 1920 West Virginia miners' strike and, after serving years, was deported to Italy in July 1925 — his family left behind on ILD relief. The Labor Defender told his story as a warning of what deportation added to the class-war prisoner's sentence.
